title: Al-Mubdi', the Originator
tomorrow: He begins it. then what does the Qur'an say He does?

cards: A blank document with the cursor blinking. A notebook nobody has written in yet. The first morning at a new job.
Beginnings are their own kind of hard. Before the first word, a Muslim may say one short phrase: bismillah, in the name of God. Before a meal, a drive, an essay.
Today's Name is the reason it fits so well. Al-Mubdi', the Originator, the one who begins.

teach.b: One question today: who makes the first move?

The Qur'an's answer, in Surah Yunus, in Pickthall's English: "Lo! He produceth creation, then reproduceth it." Where Pickthall writes produceth, the Arabic is the verb of beginning, from the same family as Al-Mubdi'.
So when someone says bismillah over a plate of rice, it's a small way of saying: this beginning is borrowed from the Beginner. Here's where a neighbor sounds close.
The Bible's first line, which Jews and Christians both read, says in the King James Version: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth."

A Christian grandmother saying grace over a meal and a Muslim saying bismillah over the same meal are doing something alike: putting God at the start. That's shared, and it's worth noticing at a crowded table.
And here's an honest difference. The Bible opens on the story of creation, told on its very first page.
The Qur'an opens with a prayer, al-Fatiha, and speaks of the beginning inside other surahs, and in Surah Yunus the beginning comes paired with a second act.
Two scriptures, each in its own words, and neither one is the other with new spelling. The first move, both say, isn't ours.

how: Muslims say bismillah before eating, traveling, studying and other beginnings, and as they begin reading the Qur'an; Al-Mubdi' is called on among the Names.

o: the Planner who sees the end first
the Builder who finishes what others start

s: the Qur'an opens with a creation story, like Genesis
it opens with al-Fatiha, a prayer, and speaks of creation's beginning in other surahs.
the Bible's first line is 'In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth'
Genesis 1:1, read by Jews and Christians alike.
bismillah is said only before reading the Qur'an
it's said before a meal, a drive, an essay: any beginning.

games.q: you start a group project with friends from three different faiths. someone suggests everybody open the first meeting 'the same way.' what fits today's lesson?
o: pick one prayer for everyone; the words all mean the same thing anyway.
let each begin in their own words, or in silence: the first move is shared, the words aren't.
skip any beginning; faith has nothing to do with a group project.
games.why: Genesis and Surah Yunus both give God the first move, in their own words. sharing the start doesn't mean making the words the same.

practice: Begin something good, and begin it small: the first line of a message you've owed someone, the first step of a plan, the first sentence on an empty page. If you'd like, say bismillah before the first word.
Then sit for the two minutes with it begun and not finished, which is allowed.

wordCard.voice: Al-Mubdi'. The Originator: the one who begins creation, and lends every small start its first breath.

orig.note: Arabic: the Originator, the one who begins. Surah Yunus uses the verb: He begins creation, then brings it back.

carryVoice: To take with you: he begins, and every small start can borrow from that. Day fifteen thirty-two, begun.
